claims.text: Retention of toughness in high-entropy alloys is governed by in-situ metastable particles that transform under mechanical loading.
The proposed initial material has a homogeneous solid-solution matrix containing uniformly dispersed in-situ metastable particles.
Tetragonal ZrO2 can serve as the metastable particle phase.
Changing Zr content and oxygen partial pressure can control the fraction and stability of metastable ZrO2 particles in a high-entropy alloy.
Room-temperature testing at sufficiently slow controlled strain rates will provide enough time for stress-induced particle transformation.
Applied mechanical stress causes metastable tetragonal ZrO2 particles to transform.
The tetragonal ZrO2 transforms martensitically into a more stable phase such as monoclinic ZrO2.
The particle transformation generates localized compressive stresses at crack tips.
Transformation of metastable particles promotes crack deflection, crack bridging, and crack branching.
The resulting crack-tip shielding delays crack propagation and enhances toughness.
High-entropy alloys with a higher fraction of metastable particles will have markedly greater fracture toughness than alloys lacking those particles.
In-situ XRD or TEM during loading should detect stress-induced phase transformation at or near crack tips.
Baseline alloys processed to suppress metastable particles are expected to have lower toughness.
Reducing Zr content or processing under low oxygen can suppress formation or retention of the metastable phase.
In baseline alloys, brittleness will correlate directly with high hardness.
The hypothesis applies only where composition and processing permit formation and stress-induced transformation of nanoscale metastable particles.
Particle size, particle distribution, or matrix bonding characteristics can inhibit the proposed transformation mechanism.
The mechanism will not operate when temperature or stress falls outside the range required for transformation kinetics.
Transformation toughening by in-situ metastable ZrO2 particles has been demonstrated in a high-entropy carbide.
Failure to observe both a statistically significant toughness increase and a stress-induced transformation in the particle-containing samples would falsify the proposed mechanism.
